strengths: Well-motivated diagnostic analysis: the paper goes beyond proposing a defense and provides an empirical investigation (attention maps, Fisher Discriminant Ratio analysis in Sec. 3.1 and Appendices D–E) of why MLLMs fail on multimodal safety — insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions — which is a genuine and interesting insight that also explains why safety prompts alone underperform.

The three-stage design is technically coherent and addresses a real trade-off: query-level continuous risk scoring plus risk-adaptive activation steering avoids the iterative refine/regenerate loops of ECSO/ETA-style defenses, and the results substantiate the efficiency claim.

Extensive and mostly convincing empirical evidence: ASR reductions on three jailbreak benchmarks (MM-SafetyBench, SPA-VL, FigStep) across four MLLMs with near-zero utility degradation on four utility benchmarks, plus throughput comparisons (Fig. 7).

Unusually thorough ablations and appendix: hyperparameter sweeps (γ, N), stage-wise ablations with binary vs. adaptive steering (Tab. 2), robustness of unsafe prototypes to query source (Tab. 5), comparison of refusal vector definitions against Arditi et al. (Tab. 6), and qualitative steering-strength analyses (Appendix H).
Clear writing, transparent hyperparameter reporting, and reproducibility/ethics statements with code release promised; appropriate attribution of data and methods.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation contamination: S_base and α are calibrated from 100 SPA-VL samples (Sec. 3.2, A.4), yet SPA-VL is also one of the three safety evaluation benchmarks. Although only two scalar parameters are derived, calibrating on the test distribution weakens the headline SPA-VL results; calibrating on a held-out or separate harmful-query distribution would be more defensible.

No evaluation against adaptive attacks. The defense relies on (i) the MLLM itself generating a visual context caption and (ii) refusal behavior appearing in the first N=3 tokens. An attacker aware of RAS could craft images that induce misleading captions, or jailbreaks whose first tokens do not resemble refusal patterns, potentially bypassing both risk evaluation and steering. The evaluation is limited to static benchmarks; no red-teaming or attack-aware robustness study is provided.

Only last-layer steering of the first three tokens may yield superficial refusals rather than deep safety alignment; the paper itself cites Qi et al. (2024) on shallow safety alignment, but does not test response-level or multi-turn probes to check whether harmful content re-emerges after the steered prefix.

Model coverage is somewhat dated: LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, Qwen-VL-Chat, and InternLM-XComposer-2.5. Results on newer, more aligned architectures (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT/OneVision, Qwen2-VL) would strengthen claims of generality.

Some circularity and external dependence in the pipeline: unsafe prototypes come from GPT-4-generated queries, and the visual context is generated by the (unsecured) MLLM itself; the paper does not analyze failure modes when the captioner misdescribes unsafe image content, which is arguably the hardest case for the method.

Minor clarity issues (e.g., grammatical slips such as 'we steers'; α determination described only implicitly) and the extra captioning forward pass is not itemized in the throughput analysis, making the 'faster inference' claim slightly less precise than it could be.

strengths: The paper is well motivated and clearly written overall, with a clean three-stage framing (query reformulation, risk evaluation, risk-adaptive steering) supported by an intuitive analysis of weak cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions (FDR analysis, attention maps, including an extended FigStep analysis in Appendix E).

Evaluation breadth is good: four MLLMs, three jailbreak benchmarks, four utility benchmarks, throughput measurements, and multiple ablations (stages, gamma/N, refusal-vector definitions, unsafe-query sources), plus qualitative steering-strength sweeps in the appendix.

The efficiency argument is credible: risk assessment on only the first three tokens and steering only the last layer yield large ASR reductions with near-zero utility loss and better throughput than ECSO/ETA (Tab. 1, Fig. 7).
Reproducibility is addressed: hyperparameters, model-specific S_base/alpha values, prototype query lists, and benchmark details are reported, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: each ingredient is established — image-to-text transformation of the query (ECSO, Gou et al. 2024, which the paper does not clearly differentiate from 'visual context'), safety prompting (FigStep, CoCA), refusal-direction steering (Arditi et al. 2024), and adaptive steering strength (Wang et al. 2025a). The main contribution is their combination plus a sigmoid-scaled steering strength, which is an incremental engineering contribution rather than a new insight or algorithm.

A serious experimental hygiene concern: S_base and alpha are calibrated on 100 samples drawn from SPA-VL, which is also one of the evaluated safety test benchmarks (Sec. 4.1, Appendix A.4). This conflates calibration data with test data and likely inflates the reported SPA-VL results relative to baselines tuned without such access.

The mechanism appears shallow by the paper's own cited evidence: alignment is applied only to the last layer and the first three response tokens, yet the paper cites Qi et al. (2024) arguing that safety alignment must be more than a few tokens deep. There is no evidence that refusal persists beyond the steered prefix, and no robustness evaluation against adaptive or multi-turn attacks that could trivially defer harmful content past token three.

Risk evaluation design is ad hoc: cosine similarity between softmax(LMHead(activation)) vectors of only three tokens against GPT-4-generated text-only prototypes is heuristic; no justification is given for why softmaxed logits are preferable to raw activations, and sensitivity to the choice of prototype set, while ablated over two sources, is not deeply analyzed.

Safety is measured only by ASR on attack benchmarks; over-refusal on adversarially benign or borderline queries (a stated motivation) is not evaluated directly — utility is measured only on benign-only benchmarks, so the precision claim is under-supported.

Generality of gains is uneven: improvements on InternLM-XComposer-2.5 are far smaller (original ASR already low, +81.2% vs +89-90% elsewhere), and the method's dependence on a fixed prompt template plus model-specific calibration raises questions about transferability to stronger, better-aligned modern MLLMs (only 2023-2024 era ~7B models are tested).

Presentation issues: grammatical slips (e.g., 'we steers'), dense figures (Fig. 2, Fig. 7 legends hard to parse), and several key details (visual-context prompt template) relegated to the appendix, which weakens the main-text self-containedness.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis: the paper does not just propose a method, but first diagnoses why MLLMs fail at multimodal safety reasoning (insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions, quantified via Fisher Discriminant Ratio and attention maps across query formulations). This analysis is convincing and reproduced across MM-Safety and FigStep (Appendix E).

The three-stage design (vision-aware query reformulation, exponentially weighted risk evaluation, risk-adaptive activation steering) is logically built on the analysis, and each design choice is empirically justified (Figs. 4-6, ablations on stages, gamma, N, and steering method in Tab. 2 and Appendix G).

Strong and comprehensive empirical evidence: four MLLMs spanning different families and sizes, three jailbreak benchmarks, four utility benchmarks, and throughput measurements. RAS achieves the largest ASR reductions (roughly +81 to +90% average gain) while maintaining utility nearly identical to the original models and delivering better inference speed than refinement-based baselines.

Thorough ablations that address obvious reviewer questions: robustness to the source of unsafe prototypes (Appendix F), comparison against the standard Arditi et al. refusal vector (Appendix G, showing the proposed per-query vector is substantially more effective), and qualitative steering-strength sweeps showing predictable, monotone behavior across models (Appendix H).

Good reproducibility practices: hyperparameters, model-specific calibration values (Tab. 3), prompt templates, and benchmark details are reported, with a code release promised; ethics and limitations are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation leakage in risk calibration: Sbase and alpha are derived from 100 SPA-VL samples (Sec. 3.2, Appendix A.4) and are then evaluated on the SPA-VL test set itself. This risks inflating SPA-VL ASR results; the paper should either calibrate on a disjoint harmful set or report sensitivity of results to this choice.

Novelty is primarily in the combination and adaptation of existing components: attention-head selection (Kang et al., 2025b), textualizing visual elements (Pandey et al., 2022), prototype-based refusal similarity, and activation steering (Arditi et al., 2024). Individually, the pieces are known; the contribution is the analysis plus the risk-adaptive integration. This is acceptable, but the claimed novelty should be framed more carefully.

Chicken-and-egg concern for visual context generation: the reformulation relies on the MLLM generating a one-sentence description that surfaces safety-critical content. If the model could reliably describe the harmful image content, one might argue it already has enough signal to refuse; the paper does not quantify how often the generated visual context is wrong or incomplete, which is a plausible failure mode on adversarial or unusual images.

Robustness to adaptive attacks is untested: an adversary aware of RAS could attempt multi-turn attacks, image perturbations that degrade the visual-context generation, or responses crafted to avoid refusal-like first tokens (since risk evaluation depends on the first N=3 tokens). The evaluation is purely on static benchmarks with MD-Judge as the sole judge; multi-judge or human verification of refusals would strengthen the safety claims.

The refusal vector v = mu_u - x_i depends on each individual query activation, so steering strength implicitly varies with the activation norm of the benign query; the paper does not analyze potential failure modes of this per-query vector formulation (e.g., queries with atypical activations) beyond aggregate ASR numbers.

Handling of the generated visual context adds an extra forward pass per query; the throughput comparison covers the full pipeline, but a breakdown of the overhead of Stage 1 vs. Stage 2/3 would clarify where the efficiency gains actually come from.

strengths: Well-motivated analysis: the paper identifies insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions as a cause of multimodal safety failures, supported by both qualitative attention maps and a quantitative FDR analysis across layers, query formulations, and multiple safe/unsafe image sources (supplementary Sec. 5-6).

The proposed MoRAS method is conceptually simple and well-designed: the three stages (vision-aware query reformulation, exponentially weighted risk evaluation, and risk-scaled activation steering) directly follow from the analysis, and the adaptive steering magnitude elegantly avoids per-model steering-strength tuning.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: safety is evaluated across five diverse jailbreak benchmarks (SPA-VL, FigStep, MM-Safety SD+Typo, JOOD, visual adversarial attacks) and utility on five benchmarks, across five MLLM backbones/sizes, with consistent improvements over prompt-based, response-refinement, and steering baselines.

Strong treatment of computational cost: pre-deployment overhead (wall-clock breakdown) and inference throughput are measured on identical hardware, and the claimed efficiency gains (126.6x less calibration time, marginal throughput loss) are substantiated with detailed breakdowns.

Extensive and careful supplementary material: ablations on every design choice (gamma, N, refusal-vector formulation, adaptive vs. fixed steering), sensitivity to calibration and unsafe-query sources, over-refusal evaluation (XSTest, OR-Bench), suffix-injection robustness, and fair hyperparameter searches for the ASTRA and AutoSteer baselines, which strengthens the credibility of the comparisons.

Appropriate attribution and reproducibility signals: prompts, calibration data sources, hardware, and model-specific parameters (Sb, alpha) are documented, and the calibration procedure is shown robust to source and scale.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is under-validated: the analysis shows that low attention to safety-critical regions correlates with low FDR and unsafe behavior, and that adding visual contexts increases both attention and separability, but this does not conclusively establish that attention deficiency is the cause of safety failures rather than a correlated symptom; alternative explanations are not ruled out.

Robustness against adaptive attacks is only lightly explored: since the visual context is generated by the same MLLM being defended, an attacker who causes the model to produce an incomplete or misleading caption could plausibly evade Stage 1; only one suffix-injection setting is tested, and a principled analysis of this failure mode is missing.

The method's safety gains on LLaVA-1.5-7B are partly attributable to the safety prompt plus visual context alone (Stage 1 achieves ASR 7.1/2.8/3.5, essentially matching the full method), so the marginal contribution of the risk-evaluation and steering stages is mainly utility recovery; this makes the pipeline's necessity on stronger baselines somewhat less clear.

Some methodological details raise questions: risk evaluation depends on sampling the first N output tokens (introducing stochasticity in the risk signal), and steering only the last layer for the first three tokens is a strong empirical choice whose justification is largely empirical rather than principled.

Modest over-refusal increases are reported (e.g., +3.2% XSTest, +4.3% OR-Bench) and are acknowledged but not further analyzed; given the paper's emphasis on preserving utility, a deeper treatment of the safety-helpfulness frontier would strengthen the claims.

Minor presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'seperable', 'for for'), and Fig. 1/attention-map evidence relies on a proxy for safety-relevant attention whose validity depends on the top-n head selection, which is only briefly justified.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated core insight: the paper identifies insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions as a cause of multimodal safety failures, and supports this with both qualitative attention maps (Fig. 1, 3, 10) and quantitative FDR analysis (Fig. 4, 12, 13), including analysis on typographic attacks (FigStep, MM-Safety) that explains why prompt-based baselines fail there.

Comprehensive empirical evidence appropriate to an Algorithms/General contribution: five diverse jailbreak benchmarks (SPA-VL, FigStep, MM-Safety, JOOD, VAA including white-box adversarial images), four MLLM backbones of different families and sizes, five strong baselines spanning all three defense paradigms, plus utility evaluation on five benchmarks.

Strong safety–utility–efficiency trade-off: MoRAS achieves the lowest or near-lowest ASR across nearly all benchmarks while matching vanilla utility (Tab. 1, 8), with only modest over-refusal increases (Tab. 9), and demonstrates substantial reductions in both pre-deployment overhead (Tab. 10, Fig. 7) and inference latency versus refinement-based defenses.

Thorough ablations and sensitivity analyses in the supplementary: stage-wise ablation (Tab. 2), hyperparameter sweeps for gamma and N (Fig. 9), robustness to unsafe-prototype and calibration-set sources (Tab. 5, 6), fixed vs. adaptive steering comparison (Tab. 12), baseline hyperparameter searches (Fig. 18, 19), and qualitative steering-strength analyses. The supplementary is extensive and supports reproducibility.

The reframing of the refusal vector as query-specific (Eq. 9) rather than a global safe-unsafe difference direction (Eq. 8 from Arditi et al.) is a substantive, well-evaluated design choice (Tab. 7) that meaningfully improves steering effectiveness.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is essentially a composition of known components — image-to-text captioning (as in ECSO), refusal-direction steering (as in Arditi et al. and ASTRA/AutoSteer), and risk-score-gated intervention (as in AutoSteer/ETA). The individual pieces are not new; the contribution lies in the attention-based diagnosis and the specific combination plus adaptive scaling, which some reviewers may view as engineering rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The vision-aware reformulation pipeline has a potential reliability and safety gap that is not analyzed: the visual context is generated by the same frozen MLLM being defended. The paper does not discuss what happens when the model refuses to caption an unsafe image, produces an incorrect or evasive caption, or when the caption itself becomes an attack surface (e.g., text-only jailbreaks against the reformulated query). Robustness of Stage 1 is asserted but not stress-tested.

Risk estimation rests on strong assumptions: refusal behavior concentrated in the first three tokens (N=3), a 50-query GPT-4 prototype set, and a sigmoid calibration centered on a sample mean Sb. Although supplementary ablations show robustness across prototype/calibration sources, these experiments are on one model (LLaVA-1.5-7B); generalization of these choices to other backbones is not demonstrated.

The core attention and FDR analysis (Figs. 3–4) is conducted only on LLaVA-1.5-7B, and the causal link between 'weak visual attention' and jailbreak success is correlational; the paper does not show, e.g., that artificially boosting attention alone reduces ASR without the steering component, which would more directly validate the central causal claim in the title.

Robustness against attacks explicitly designed for MoRAS itself (adaptive attackers aware of the caption-then-evaluate pipeline, or suffix attacks targeting the reformulated query rather than the original) is not evaluated; the suffix-injection test (Tab. 9) augments the original MM-Safety query only.

Some headline claims need qualification: the 126.6x pre-deployment overhead reduction is measured against the slowest baseline (ASTRA) in wall-clock minutes, and inference throughput comparisons conflate method-specific output-length differences (Tab. 11 shows shorter MoRAS outputs) with genuine speedup; a latency-normalized analysis would be more convincing.

strengths: Insightful and well-supported diagnosis: the paper identifies insufficient cross-modal attention to safety-critical image regions as a root cause of multimodal safety failures, and backs this with both qualitative attention maps (Figs. 1, 3, 10) and a quantitative Fisher Discriminant Ratio analysis across layers (Figs. 4, 12, 13), including ablations showing safety prompts alone do not improve separability.

The proposed MoRAS pipeline is coherent and well-motivated: vision-aware query reformulation strengthens visual grounding, exponentially weighted risk evaluation yields a continuous risk signal from only the first few tokens, and risk-scaled activation steering on the original query avoids the over-refusal pathology of the reformulated query. The ablation (Tab. 2) cleanly demonstrates why all three stages are needed.

Comprehensive empirical validation: five jailbreak benchmarks (SPA-VL, FigStep, MM-Safety SD+Typo, JOOD, and white-box VAA), five MLLM backbones across architectures and sizes, six competitive baselines spanning three method families, and utility evaluation on four general benchmarks. MoRAS achieves consistently low ASR with near-vanilla utility.

Strong efficiency evidence: pre-deployment overhead is reduced by two orders of magnitude versus ASTRA/AutoSteer (1.4 min vs. 35-472 min), with throughput analysis and a detailed overhead breakdown (Fig. 7, Tabs. 10-11).

The supplementary material is unusually thorough and strengthens the scientific case: hyperparameter sensitivity, robustness of unsafe-prototype construction and calibration to alternative data sources and scales (Tabs. 5-6), a meaningful comparison of refusal-vector formulations (Tab. 7), adaptive vs. fixed steering (Tab. 12), over-refusal evaluation on XSTest/OR-Bench, and robustness to suffix-injection attacks (Tab. 9).

Proper attribution of data, methods, and calibration protocols; ethical considerations are addressed; no contribution type is declared, but the work is well-framed under Algorithms/General with appropriate applied-systems evidence.
weaknesses: Per-component technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines image captioning, prototype-based output similarity, and refusal-direction steering, all of which exist in prior work; the main novelty lies in the attention-based analysis, the query-adaptive refusal vector, and the risk-scaled, utility-preserving integration. This is acceptable for Algorithms/General, but the contribution rests primarily on empirical rather than conceptual novelty.

Dependence on self-generated visual contexts introduces a potential adaptive-attack surface: an adversary could craft images that elicit benign-sounding captions, misleading the risk evaluator. The paper evaluates gradient-based visual attacks and suffix injection, but no explicitly caption-aware adaptive attack; this gap deserves discussion or evaluation.

The reported ASR reduction (19.4% average on LLaVA-1.5-7B) is dominated by baseline comparisons; against the strongest steering baselines the gap varies by benchmark (e.g., AutoSteer is comparable or better on several SPA-VL/VAA settings for some models), so claims of consistent superiority should be stated with care.

Methods rely on an external judge (MD-Judge) for ASR and GPT-based scoring for MM-Vet; additionally, supplementary hyperparameter searches switch the judge to GPT-4o due to cost, which slightly weakens direct comparability of those auxiliary results.

Over-refusal, while modest, does increase (7.2% vs. 4.0% on XSTest; 27.7% vs. 23.4% on OR-Bench), and several core hyperparameters (γ, N, choice of last-layer steering) were selected by sweeping; the sensitivity analysis mitigates this concern but the method is not entirely tuning-free.

The core steering is applied only at the last layer and to the first N tokens; the paper's own supplementary results suggest intermediate-layer steering could matter, and the design choice is justified empirically rather than analytically.
